name: CoDiPack (operator-overloading AD, expression templates)
baseline: ADOL-C and Adept (other C++ operator-overloading AD tools); none of the listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor) apply
workload: Tape recording and reversal time and tape memory for a coupled Burgers-equation PDE test and for SU2 CFD (inviscid flow over the LM1021 supersonic aircraft), versus Adept and ADOL-C, with GCC and Intel compilers (per the TOMS paper as described by search results; paper not opened).
claimed_speedup: Paper reports CoDiPack roughly on par with Adept with slightly faster tape recording and reversal and about 7% (250 MB) less memory, and faster than ADOL-C; exact factors could not be verified because the paper pages were blocked (see caveats for unverified snippet numbers).
stars_or_usage: 119 stars; evaluated on the SU2 CFD suite in its paper and reported (search snippets) in the ISSM ice-sheet model; developed at TU Kaiserslautern (RPTU)
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++17 (2.x release for C++11). GPL-3.0 (other licensing on request), so linking proprietary code needs a commercial arrangement. Operator overloading with expression templates: needs the active type substituted into the code, tapes cost memory proportional to the number of operations, and performance depends on forced inlining (-DCODI_UseForcedInlines recommended in the README). Several tape types (RealReverse, RealReverseIndex, RealReversePrimal, RealReversePrimalIndex) trade memory against generality.
caveats: I could not open the evidence: the README of the repo (opened) cites the peer-reviewed paper 'High-Performance Derivative Computations using CoDiPack' (Sagebaum, Albring, Gauger, ACM TOMS 45(4), 2019, doi 10.1145/3356900, arXiv 1709.07229), but dl.acm.org, arxiv.org, ar5iv, researchgate, arxiv-vanity, groundai and scicomp.rptu.de were all blocked by the egress proxy. Everything below about numbers comes from web-search result snippets and is UNVERIFIED: (a) CoDiPack vs Adept performance quite similar, CoDiPack slightly faster at recording and reversal and 7% (250 MB) less memory; (b) SU2 LM1021 test with 5,730,841 interior elements: relative runtime factors of 3.1 to 4.47 for recording and 0.4 to 0.86 for interpretation of one flow iteration without preaccumulation (baseline of that ratio not confirmed); (c) an independent third-party paper (AD-HOC, arXiv 2412.05300, snippet only) lists first-order derivative-to-primal runtime ratios ADOL-C 8.36x, dco/c++ 3.03x, CoDiPack 3.63x, i.e. CoDiPack about 2.3x faster than ADOL-C there (derived from snippet data). Hardware, compiler versions and flags are unknown. The repo itself has no benchmark directory (tests/ has events, functional, general only) and its README and docs make no numeric performance claim. Tier B rests on peer review only; a verifier able to open the paper should confirm the numbers, the CPU model and the flags, which could move this to A (benchmark code for the paper may not be public) or down to C. Not a numerical-kernel library of the listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor): competes with other AD tools, so category fit is loose.

name: Clad (Clang-plugin source-transformation AD)
baseline: Enzyme (LLVM-level AD, run through Clad's own use_enzyme backend); Tapenade planned; none of the listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor) apply
workload: Google Benchmark micro-benchmarks in the repo comparing Clad-generated reverse-mode and vector-forward-mode gradients with Enzyme-generated gradients of small functions (array add and multiply, sum), plus Hessian, matrix, tape, multithreading, GPT-2 training (cladtorch) and LULESH and XSBench (CUDA) benchmarks. No results are published.
claimed_speedup: No numbers found: neither the README, the docs (CoreConcepts, FAQ, UsingEnzymeWithinClad, ReleaseNotes) nor the opened repo pages state any speedup or timing versus Adept, CppAD, CoDiPack or Enzyme.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmarks target is built in release mode; GPT2Training is built with -O3 -ffast-math (from benchmark/CMakeLists.txt); no results to attach flags to.
stars_or_usage: 421 stars, 212 forks; reported (search results) as used in ROOT/RooFit at CERN
tradeoffs: Compiler plugin: needs a matching Clang/LLVM (14.0.x to 23.2.x per README), differentiates only code visible to Clang at compile time (custom derivatives needed for external functions), and supports a growing but incomplete set of C++ features. Source transformation can expose optimizations to the compiler, but reverse mode stores intermediates on a tape (memory grows with operation count). LGPL-3.0.
caveats: Evidence-free record: the repo ships benchmark code (benchmark/EnzymeCladComparison.cpp, Hessians.cpp, VectorModeComparison.cpp, GPT2Training.cpp, LULESH_diff.patch, XSBench_diff.patch, benchmark_compare.py) but no committed results; issue #1764 says release builds had yielded 0 ns because the optimizer removed code, and PR #1771 added benchmark::DoNotOptimize to repair that (Tapenade comparison still only proposed). The Clad-vs-Enzyme benchmark compares two backends of Clad itself. Search-result snippets (papers and ROOT blog pages, all blocked, unverified) mention Clad speedups of roughly 2x to 29x versus numerical (finite-difference) differentiation in RooFit and TFormula, which is not an AD-tool or listed baseline. The claim that source transformation is faster than operator overloading (ADOL-C, CppAD, Adept) appears in snippets without numbers. Tier D kept per the seed-pass rule although the repo has fewer than 1k stars; the project is widely referenced (ROOT).

name: midint-arithmetic (Oancea/Watt GPU midsize-integer add and multiply)
baseline: CGBN (NVIDIA CUDA Cooperative Groups Big Numbers); GMP is used only to validate results, not timed
workload: Batched block-level big-integer addition (1-Add and 6-Add, GB/s) and quadratic multiplication (1-Mul = a*b; Poly = (a*a+b)*(b*b+b)+a*b) on an A100, precision 2^12 to 2^19 bits with the instance count chosen so bits x instances = 2^32, hand-written CUDA prototype ('CudaP', the cuda/ folder of this repo) versus CGBN.
claimed_speedup: Quadratic multiplication: CGBN is slower than CudaP by 1.21x at 2^16 bits, 4.48x at 2^17 and 35.1x at 2^18 (1-Mul); Poly 1.22x, 21.0x and 49.9x at the same sizes; CGBN is equal or slightly faster at 2^12 to 2^14 bits (CGBN/CudaP 0.91 to 1.01 on 1-Mul). Addition 1-Add (GB/s, CudaP vs CGBN): 1046 vs 369 at 2^18 bits, 1209 vs 368 at 2^17, 1358 vs 376 at 2^16, i.e. about 2.8x, 3.3x and 3.6x (derived from page data); comparable at 2^12 to 2^13 bits. Abstract of the Springer paper: outperforms CGBN above 32K bits, comparable below. Division (fork code): CGBN is 3.64x to 7.36x faster at 2^13 to 2^15 bits and does not support larger sizes.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_80 (from cuda/Makefile and cuda/cgbn-tests/Makefile, both linked with -lgmp); nvcc and CUDA versions not stated; paper text says RHEL 8.10
hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPU (6912 cores, 1555 GB/s peak bandwidth, 19.5 TFLOP/s FP32) per the preprint; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: NVIDIA GPU only (CUDA, sm_80 tuned); operates on integers that fit one CUDA block (about 2^12 to 2^19 bits, about 410,000 bits max after the erratum for the FFT path) and needs large batches (instances = 2^32 / bits) to fill the GPU, so it is not a single-number latency replacement for GMP. Contains an outdated early Futhark version (futhark-ninja) and a Futhark version (futhark-reg) that needs an archived custom Futhark compiler tarball. Addition, subtraction, multiplication only in the CUDA folder; division lives in the Futhark folder and in the separate division fork.
caveats: Same research codebase as the already-listed fork aske0778/midint-arithmetic-division, which is the parent's fork adding CUDA division (CASC 2026 paper [33] by Marchioro, Raahauge, Lovenskjold, Oancea, Watt; the fork's own GMP numbers, 11.3x at 2^18 bits and so on, come from arXiv 2606.06386 which I could not open). This parent repo's evidence is versus CGBN, not GMP or MPFR, so it is off the listed baselines. The numbers I quote are from the repo's own preprint 'High-Level Big Integer Arithmetic in Futhark for GPUs' (submitted to SYNASC per the README, tables I to III, opened as a PDF via raw.githubusercontent.com), whose 'CudaP' columns are the cuda/ prototype of the Springer essay 'GPU Implementations for Midsize Integer Addition and Multiplication' (LNCS essays for Alan Mycroft, pp. 51-79, doi 10.1007/978-3-032-08187-2_4, published as a Springer essay-volume chapter; arXiv 2405.14642 not opened). First-party results (the authors compare their own prototype with CGBN); CGBN is a 2018 beta and is far faster for small sizes and division, so the win applies only above 2^15 bits. No LICENSE file in the repo (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt, COPYING all 404) so code is reference only. README erratum: FFT prime fields use 10 of 16 and 25 of 32 bits, lowering max precision (PrimeField64 about 410,000 bits). Tier A given public benchmark code, nvcc flags in the Makefile and A100 stated, though nvcc version and host CPU are missing; the results table is in a preprint, not a committed results file.

name: MultiFloats.hpp (dzhang314/MultiprecisionBenchmarks)
baseline: MPFR (also GMP mpf, CLN, FLINT, Boost.Multiprecision, QD, CAMPARY, libquadmath in the same harness)
workload: Google Benchmark kernels axpy, dot, gemv and gemm on arrays of extended-precision numbers (axpy and dot 2^8 to 2^24 elements, gemm n = 8 to 512), OpenMP thread counts 1 to 32, at 1 to 4 double-word expansions (MPFR run at 53, 103, 156 and 208 bits) with MultiFloats.hpp using hand-vectorized (8-wide) code on split-array storage.
claimed_speedup: Per the SC25 paper abstract as returned by web search (paper itself not opened): up to 35.6x over MPFR, 11.7x over QD, 34.4x over CAMPARY and 41.4x over FLINT (orchestrator lead adds Zen 5; unverified). The repo commits no result files.
compiler_and_flags: g++-14 and clang++-20, -std=c++17 -fopenmp -ffp-contract=off -fno-math-errno -O3 -march=native -flto -fvisibility=hidden -fmerge-all-constants (-fwhole-program for GCC), linked with -lbenchmark; from build_linux.sh in the repo
stars_or_usage: 2 stars (benchmark repo); the algorithms are also in MultiFloats.jl with 159 stars
tradeoffs: Fixed expansions of 2 to 4 doubles (about 2x to 4x double precision, roughly 106 to 212 bits) with the exponent range of double; not arbitrary precision and not correctly rounded like MPFR. Header MultiFloats.hpp (multifloats/ folder) uses x86 SSE/AVX/AVX-512 intrinsics and an ARM variant (multifloats-arm) where NEON was disabled in the latest commits. Designed for data-parallel kernels; scalar single-operation latency gains are not the claim.
caveats: Could not open the evidence: the SC '25 paper (Zhang and Aiken, 'High-Performance Branch-Free Algorithms for Extended-Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic', doi 10.1145/3712285.3759876, pp. 695-710) and its hosts (dl.acm.org, theory.stanford.edu, springer, dkzhang.com, purl.stanford.edu) were blocked; the speedup figures are from a search-result snippet of the abstract and the CPU model, thread count and kernel behind '35.6x' are unverified. The repo is only the harness: README is a one-line title and no benchmark JSON outputs are committed (bench_linux.sh writes MultiFloats-GCC-32.json style files at OMP_NUM_THREADS 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 but none are in the tree), so a reader must build and run it (needs Google Benchmark, GMP, MPFR, CLN, FLINT, Boost, QD, CAMPARY via download_campary.sh) to reproduce. Comparison fairness: MultiFloats kernels are hand-vectorized on split arrays while MPFR and GMP are scalar per-element calls with per-thread temporaries; MPFR is correctly rounded with a huge exponent range. Tier B (peer-reviewed) rather than A because the CPU model and committed results could not be confirmed; if the paper states the CPU model and flags, A is justified since the harness and flags are public. The same algorithms are verified in Rocq (MultiFloatProofs) per the author profile.

name: wjr (WJR big integer and utility library)
baseline: GMP (mpn_* low-level functions in the repo's own benchmark)
workload: Google Benchmark micro-benchmarks in benchmarks/src/biginteger.cpp: wjr addc_1, addc_n, subc_1, subc_n, mul_1, addmul_1, submul_1, addlsh_n, rsblsh_n, mul, sqr, div_qr and biginteger to/from chars against the GMP mpn_add_1, mpn_add_n, mpn_sub_n, mpn_mul_1, mpn_addmul_1, mpn_submul_1, mpn_lshift/rshift counterparts (built with WJR_USE_GMP); no results published.
claimed_speedup: No numbers found: the README (Chinese), docs/modules/README.md, issues (none open) and the PR pages (#13, #20) contain no speedup versus GMP. CI (benchmarks.yml, weekly) uploads benchmark-results.json artifacts and a regression summary versus the previous run, not versus GMP, and runs without GMP in the default core profile.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release with -march=native for non-MSVC (CMakeLists.txt); compiler not stated; optional NASM assembly modules for x64
hardware: CI uses ubuntu-24.04 GitHub-hosted runners; no CPU model stated
tradeoffs: C++17, 64-bit only, most optimizations x64-only, AMD not tuned (TODO list), exception handling poorly supported, JSON wrapper not zero-overhead. LGPL-2.1. Bundles biginteger, json, string, ring_buffer and other modules; README is in Chinese.
caveats: Evidence-free record: the harness exists (benchmarks/src/biginteger.cpp has wjr_, fallback_ and gmp_ prefixed cases and benchmarks/tools/compare.py plots wjr vs fallback vs gmp from Google Benchmark JSON) but no numbers are published anywhere I could open (README, docs, issues, PR descriptions, workflow runs page showing only durations; wjr-z.github.io coverage page is blocked). The default CI profile builds without GMP, and the 'all' profile with GMP uses 1 repetition and 0.03 s min time (benchmarks.yml), so CI is a regression tracker, not a GMP shootout. Tier D kept per the seed-pass rule although the repo has fewer than 1k stars. A reader must build with -DWJR_BUILD_BENCHMARKS=ON -DWJR_BENCHMARK_PROFILE=all and libgmp to get numbers.
